title: Air compressor: get the motor, pump head, tank and pressure switch
summary: An air compressor gives a strong motor, a piston pump head, a steel air tank, a pressure switch, gauges, valves, hose and often a start capacitor. Allow about an hour, and a helper for the heavy parts. The main danger is stored pressure: empty the tank and prove it is empty before you loosen anything, and never cut, weld or drill the tank.

steps.text: Make it dead. Unplug the machine from the wall. If it is wired in, switch it off at the breaker and prove the supply dead (see safety_mains_isolation). On a petrol-engine unit, close the fuel valve and pull the spark plug lead. Let a pump that has just run cool for at least 30 minutes.
steps.warn: The pressure switch can start the motor by itself at any time while the plug is in, even when the machine looks idle. The pump head and outlet pipe stay hot after running.

steps.text: Drain the tank. Wear eye protection and stand to one side of the drain valve at the bottom of the tank, not in front of it. Open the valve slowly and let all the air out. It can take several minutes, and rusty water comes out first. Then pull the ring on the safety valve once. Leave the drain valve open.
steps.warn: Air at 8–12 bar fires rust, water and grit at your eyes. Never undo a fitting while the tank might still hold air.

steps.text: Prove it is empty. The tank gauge should read zero and you should hear no air at the drain or the safety valve. Don't trust the gauge alone: a clogged gauge port or drain can read zero or look empty while the tank is still full. Wait until every hiss has stopped.
steps.warn: A rusted-up drain can look open while the tank is still full. If the gauge shows pressure and nothing comes from the drain, pull the safety valve ring and keep venting. Don't unscrew anything.

steps.text: Take the cover off the pressure switch and the motor terminal box. Photograph every wire, label each with tape and disconnect them. Find the start and run capacitors (cylinders or boxes on the motor). Discharge them with a resistor tool and check with a meter before touching any terminal (see safety_discharge_capacitor).
steps.warn: A motor capacitor can hold a mains-level charge for days after unplugging.

steps.text: With the tank open to the air, unscrew the pressure switch, the gauges, the regulator, the safety valve, the check valve and the drain valve. Put the wrench on the fitting body, not on the thin tube. Keep the small unloader tube that runs from the check valve to the switch.
steps.warn: The safety valve is the only thing that stops overpressure. Never plug it, block it or remove it from a system you reuse.

steps.text: Oil-lubricated pump: before you lift it, take out the oil drain plug (or tip the pump toward the fill hole) and drain the crankcase into a pan. Wear gloves. Oil-free pumps have none. Keep the oil in a closed container as light machine oil.

Separate pump and motor. Portable direct-drive units: the pump and motor sit as one block on top of the tank, held by 4 bolts through the base plate. Belt-drive units: take off the belt guard, loosen the motor base bolts, slip the V-belt off the flywheel, then unbolt motor and pump separately. Disconnect the discharge tube and check valve line first.
steps.warn: Pump and motor together can weigh 15–35 kg and are top-heavy. Use a second person and support the load as the last bolt comes out (see safety_lifting). Keep fingers out of the belt and flywheel.

steps.text: Keep the V-belt and both pulleys. Loosen each pulley's setscrew or clamp bolt with a hex key and pull it off its shaft. Keep the shaft key with its pulley.

Check the pump and motor. Turn the pump flywheel by hand: it should turn with the soft pulse of a piston. Grinding or sticking means a worn or seized pump. Turn the motor shaft: it should be smooth. Read the nameplate for volts, power and speed (see skill_read_nameplate). Keep the motor and the capacitors it came with together.

The tank: look inside with a torch through a valve port. Thick flaking rust, deep pits or standing water mean it is no longer fit to hold pressure. Keep it open to the air from now on. Kept whole, it is still a thick steel barrel for non-food storage.
steps.warn: Don't cut, drill or weld a tank (see compressed gas). Oil mist inside can explode, even in an empty one.

steps.text: Hose and fittings: coil the hose and check along its length for cracks and bulges. Take the quick couplers, the brass fittings and the regulator. Most use a 1/4 inch pipe thread, so they fit one another.

notes:
## What's worth keeping and why

- **Motor.** A strong induction motor (1–5 hp) from a stationary or belt-drive unit, or a universal motor from a small portable. Use it to drive a saw, grinder, water pump or mill. Keep the capacitors with an induction motor: it won't start without its start capacitor.
- **Pump head.** A piston pump. Driven slowly by hand or by another motor it inflates tyres or charges a small air tank. It needs its check valve.
- **Tank.** Steel air receiver, 20–300 L. Don't reuse it for air unless it is clean inside, rust-free, and fitted with a working safety valve and gauge. Otherwise keep it whole as a barrel for rainwater or non-food storage. Not for drinking water: rust and oil.
- **Pressure switch.** Switches the motor on and off between two pressures. Air compressor switches are set for roughly 90–125 psi, too high for a water pump system. Keep it to switch another compressor.
- **Safety valve, check valve, gauges, regulator.** Reuse only in air systems.
- **Hose and couplers.** Air hose and brass quick couplers fit many other jobs, such as a blower or a water-line adaptor.
- **Capacitors.** Motor start and run capacitors. Match their label (µF and volts) to the motor you pair them with.

## Variations

- Small oil-free pancake and hot-dog compressors use a brush-type universal motor and no capacitor. If the motor is worn, see repair_motor_brushes.
- Belt-drive twin-cylinder units have a cast-iron pump with an oil sight glass and a big flywheel with fan blades.
- Petrol-engine compressors: drain the fuel first (see safety_fuel_handling).
- Tyre inflators at gas stations and dental compressors in clinics hold the same parts. Dental compressors add a dryer.

## What to leave

- A tank that is thin, pitted or rusted through, or that has a bulge or a dent.
- A cracked or hardened air hose.
- Old compressor oil that has gone black and gritty.
